claim: Human HD brain reveals upregulated lysosomal biogenesis and relatively normal autophagy flux in early Vonsattel grade brains.
source: Our recent evaluation of the autophagic-lysosomal pathway (ALP) in human HD brain reveals upregulated lysosomal biogenesis and relatively normal autophagy flux in early Vonsattel grade brains, but impaired autolysosome clearance in late grade brains, suggesting that autophagy stimulation could have therapeutic benefits as an early clinical intervention.
evidence: This is based on the authors' recent study (Berg et al., 2024) cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: ALP alterations in Q175 models are late-onset but milder compared to late-stage human HD striatum.

evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of data from Q175 mice and human HD brain (Berg et al., 2024).

evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1C1, C2, and C3.

source: To assess HTT molecular species in the Q175 mouse brain, we employed multiple antibodies that preferentially detected mHTT over wild-type HTT, including MAB1574 (Clone 1C2) (Figure 1C1 and C2), its epitope containing a 38-glns stretch (Trottier et al., 1995), and mAb PHP2 (Figure 1C1), reacting with the peptide sequence QAQPLLPQP within the proline-rich domain of HTT (Ko et al., 2018). Both detected full-length mHTT and a~120 kDa fragment in the Q175 model (Figure 1C1; 1C2 left and 1C3 top two graphs).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1C1 and C3.

claim: MAB5490 detected both wild type and mutant forms of HTT.
source: By contrast, MAB5490 (Figure 1C2 right), reacting with aa115-129 of HTT (C-terminal to the region of polyQ stretch-containing exon 1), detected both wild type and mutant forms of HTT (Figure 1C3, bottom right graph).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1C2 and C3.

claim: A ~48 kDa HTT fragment was detected by both MAB1574 and MAB5490 antibodies in some samples.
source: A~48 kDa HTT fragment may correspond to the 45–48 kDa fragment seen in human brain (Berg et al., 2024), and was detected by both MAB1574 and MAB5490 antibodies in some samples (Figure 1C2) but its levels in the Q175 models and the control TRGL were not statistically significantly different (Figure 1C3, bottom left graph).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1C2 and C3.

claim: The levels of the ~48 kDa HTT fragment in the Q175 models and the control TRGL were not statistically significantly different.
source: A~48 kDa HTT fragment may correspond to the 45–48 kDa fragment seen in human brain (Berg et al., 2024), and was detected by both MAB1574 and MAB5490 antibodies in some samples (Figure 1C2) but its levels in the Q175 models and the control TRGL were not statistically significantly different (Figure 1C3, bottom left graph).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1C3.

claim: The result suggests that HTT fragmentation is not obvious in the Q175 brains, unlike the far more prevalent occurrence of this phenomenon in human HD striatum.
source: Thus, the result suggests that HTT fragmentation is not obvious in the Q175 brains, unlike the far more prevalent occurrence of this phenomenon in human HD striatum.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the western blotting findings comparing mouse and human HD.

claim: In Q175 mice, mHTT/Ub or Ub/p62 signals were highly colocalized in IBs, particularly in NIIs, in striatal neurons.
source: Our earlier study in human HD brains Berg et al., 2024 found a high degree of colocalization of mHTT/Ub or Ub/p62 colocalized signals in IBs, suggesting a relationship between mHTT and the autophagy machinery since p62 and Ub are adaptor proteins mediating autophagic cargo sequestration. Similarly, in Q175 mice, mHTT/Ub or Ub/p62 signals were highly colocalized in IBs, particularly in NIIs, in striatal neurons of Q175 mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Triple IF labeling experiments identified IBs positive for mHTT, p62, and Ub within or outside the nuclei in Q175 mice.
source: Additional triple IF labeling experiments (mHTT/Ub/p62) with brain sections from 6- and 10-mo-old Q175 mice identified IBs positive for mHTT, p62, and Ub within or outside the nuclei (Figure 2A, arrows and arrowheads, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The 10-mo-old Q175 mice exhibited more and larger mHTT-positive IBs than 6-mo mutants.
source: The 10-mo-old Q175 mice exhibited more and larger mHTT-positive IBs than 6-mo mutants (Figure 2A, first column), consistent with Figure 1A and the literature (Carty et al., 2015; Deng et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and consistent with prior studies (Carty et al., 2015; Deng et al., 2021).

claim: The data demonstrate a close spatial relationship among mHTT and autophagy receptor protein p62 and Ub in the Q175 model, which is consistent with observations in human HD brain.
source: Thus, our data demonstrate a close spatial relationship among mHTT and autophagy receptor protein p62 and Ub in the Q175 model, which is consistent with our observations in human HD brain (Berg et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a summary of the immunofluorescence findings and comparison to human HD brain (Berg et al., 2024).

claim: Double IF labeling of mHTT with CTSD detected small punctate mHTT signal in CTSD-positive vesicles, suggesting a pool of mHTT within the ALP.
source: Double IF labeling of mHTT with a LY marker CTSD (Figure 2B1) detected small punctate mHTT signal in CTSD-positive vesicles, suggesting a pool of mHTT within the ALP.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B1.

claim: IEM with antibody MAB1574 clearly demonstrated that the AVs in either cell bodies, dendrites, and axons were labeled with concentrated silver-enhanced gold particles.
source: Consistent with this LM finding, IEM with antibody MAB1574 directed against mHTT clearly demonstrated that the AVs in either cell bodies, dendrites, and axons were labeled with concentrated silver-enhanced gold particles (Figure 2B2), and the specificity of the IEM labeling was very high, as reflected by a much higher number of silver-enhanced gold particles associated with AVs versus the minimal number of silver-enhanced gold particles with mitochondria that represent the background labeling (Figure 2B3).
evidence: This is supported by IEM data shown in Figure 2B2 and B3.

claim: The specificity of the IEM labeling for mHTT in AVs was very high, as reflected by a much higher number of silver-enhanced gold particles associated with AVs versus mitochondria.
source: Consistent with this LM finding, IEM with antibody MAB1574 directed against mHTT clearly demonstrated that the AVs in either cell bodies, dendrites, and axons were labeled with concentrated silver-enhanced gold particles (Figure 2B2), and the specificity of the IEM labeling was very high, as reflected by a much higher number of silver-enhanced gold particles associated with AVs versus the minimal number of silver-enhanced gold particles with mitochondria that represent the background labeling (Figure 2B3).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative IEM data shown in Figure 2B3.

claim: The LM and IEM findings suggest that mHTT molecules exist within ALP vesicles in the absence of definable aggresome/IB structures.
source: Together, the LM and IEM findings suggest that mHTT molecules exist within ALP vesicles in the absence of definable aggresome/IB structures, similar to the IEM finding from a recent report (Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunofluorescence and IEM findings, consistent with a prior study (Zhou et al., 2021).

claim: Pilot studies in young TRGL/Q175 mice (2.5–6-mo of age) hardly detected autophagy alterations, compared to the control TRGL mice.
source: We crossed TRGL mice (Lee et al., 2019) with Q175 to generate TRGL/Q175 and assessed AV/LY subtypes in striatal neurons with a hue angle-based analysis method (Lee et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2022). Our pilot studies in young TRGL/Q175 mice (2.5–6-mo of age) hardly detected autophagy alterations, compared to the control TRGL mice (not shown).
evidence: This is based on pilot studies conducted by the authors.

claim: Previous studies reported that autophagy impairment was hardly detected in 6-mo Q175/GFP-LC3 mice.
source: Previous studies have reported that autophagy impairment was hardly detected in 6-mo Q175/GFP-LC3 mice (Wold et al., 2016), but alterations in a limited number of autophagy markers (e.g. protein levels of p62, LC3, p-Beclin-1) were found in brain homogenates of 12–15-mo Q175 mice (Abd-Elrahman et al., 2017; Heikkinen et al., 2021; Wold et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Wold et al., 2016).

claim: Alterations in a limited number of autophagy markers (e.g. protein levels of p62, LC3, p-Beclin-1) were found in brain homogenates of 12–15-mo Q175 mice.
source: Previous studies have reported that autophagy impairment was hardly detected in 6-mo Q175/GFP-LC3 mice (Wold et al., 2016), but alterations in a limited number of autophagy markers (e.g. protein levels of p62, LC3, p-Beclin-1) were found in brain homogenates of 12–15-mo Q175 mice (Abd-Elrahman et al., 2017; Heikkinen et al., 2021; Wold et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Abd-Elrahman et al., 2017; Heikkinen et al., 2021; Wold et al., 2016).

claim: Confocal images from 17-mo-old TRGL/Q175 showed enhanced mRFP- and eGFP-LC3 signals in the striatal neurons compared to TRGL.
source: Confocal images from 17-mo-old TRGL/Q175 and control TRGL brain sections, triple-fluorescent labeled via an additional immunostaining with an anti-CTSD antibody and far-red emitting fluorophore, showed enhanced mRFP- and eGFP-LC3 signals in the striatal neurons of TRGL/Q175 compared to TRGL (Figure 3A1).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A1.

claim: Hue angle-based analysis confirmed significant increases in the numbers of AL and poorly-acidified AL (pa-AL) in 17-mo-old TRGL/Q175 compared to TRGL.
source: Hue angle-based analysis confirmed the above observations by revealing significant increases in the numbers of AL and poorly-acidified AL (pa-AL, as explained in Lee et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2022). It also detected a reduction in the number of LY (Figure 3A2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis data shown in Figure 3A2.

claim: Hue angle-based analysis detected a reduction in the number of LY in 17-mo-old TRGL/Q175 compared to TRGL.
source: Hue angle-based analysis confirmed the above observations by revealing significant increases in the numbers of AL and poorly-acidified AL (pa-AL, as explained in Lee et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2022). It also detected a reduction in the number of LY (Figure 3A2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis data shown in Figure 3A2.

claim: These results indicate that the tfLC3 reporter can reveal alterations in the proportions of AV/LY subtypes in Q175, consistent with delayed and/or deficient acidification of AL causing deficits in the reformation of LY to replenish the LY pool.
source: Thus, these results indicate that the tfLC3 reporter can reveal alterations in the proportions of AV/LY subtypes in Q175, consistent with delayed and/or deficient acidification of AL causing deficits in the reformation of LY to replenish the LY pool.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hue angle-based analysis findings.

claim: A decreased level of a mTOR substrate, p-p70S6K (T389), was observed in TRGL/Q175 compared to the control TRGL.
source: At the stage of autophagy induction signaling, we did not see alterations in the levels of mTOR and p-mTOR forms including its auto-phospho-form at S2481, but we did observe a decreased level of a mTOR substrate, p-p70S6K (T389), in TRGL/Q175 compared to the control TRGL (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), implying reduced mTOR activity, similar to the finding from a previous study (Ravikumar et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The decreased level of p-p70S6K (T389) implies reduced mTOR activity, similar to the finding from a previous study.
source: At the stage of autophagy induction signaling, we did not see alterations in the levels of mTOR and p-mTOR forms including its auto-phospho-form at S2481, but we did observe a decreased level of a mTOR substrate, p-p70S6K (T389), in TRGL/Q175 compared to the control TRGL (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), implying reduced mTOR activity, similar to the finding from a previous study (Ravikumar et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the western blotting findings, consistent with a prior study (Ravikumar et al., 2004).

claim: There was an increase in the level of total ULK1, resulting in a reduced ratio of p-ULK1 (S757)/total ULK1 in TRGL/Q175 compared to TRGL.
source: Another mTOR substrate, p-ULK1 (S757), did not exhibit changes in TRGL/Q175. However, there was an increase in the level of total ULK1, resulting in a reduced ratio of p-ULK1 (S757)/total ULK1 in TRGL/Q175 compared to TRGL (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The data collectively imply a down-regulated mTOR activity in TRGL/Q175, as expected in response to accumulated aggregate-prone protein in Q175 mice, or as a result of sequestration of mTOR by mHTT IBs.
source: The data collectively imply a down-regulated mTOR activity, as expected in response to accumulated aggregate-prone protein in Q175 mice, or as a result of sequestration of mTOR by mHTT IBs, as suggested previously (Ravikumar et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the western blotting findings, consistent with a prior study (Ravikumar et al., 2004).

claim: No statistically significant differences were detected between TRGL/Q175 and the control TRGL in all other tested marker proteins in the downstream phases of the ALP.
source: Except for these alterations, we did not detect statistically significant differences between TRGL/Q175 and the control TRGL in all other tested marker proteins in the downstream phases of the ALP (Figure 3—figure supplements 2-4).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2-4.

claim: No statistically significant alterations were detected in the levels of Beclin-1, VPS34, and ATG14 and their corresponding phosphor-forms in TRGL/Q175 compared to TRGL.
source: Of special interest is the ATG14-containing VPS34/Beclin-1 complex implicated in HD pathogenesis (Park et al., 2016; Wold et al., 2016) for which we did not detect statistically significant alterations in the levels of Beclin-1, VPS34, and ATG14 and their corresponding phosphor-forms.
evidence: This is based on western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Even if some TRGL/Q175 clearly exhibited diminished signals for p-ATG14 (S29), no statistical significance could be established due to large variations among samples.
source: Notably, even if some TRGL/Q175 clearly exhibited diminished signals for p-ATG14 (S29) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), no statistical significance could be established due to large variations among samples (See Discussion).
evidence: This is based on western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: No alterations were found in levels of full-length proteins or fragments of autophagy adaptor proteins such as p62, TRAF6 in TRGL/Q175, in contrast to immunoblot analysis of human HD brains.
source: Another notable point is that we did not find alterations in levels of full-length proteins or fragments (Jamilloux et al., 2018; Norman et al., 2010; Sanchez-Garrido et al., 2018; Valionyte et al., 2022) of autophagy adaptor proteins such as p62, TRAF6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), in contrast to our immunoblot analysis of human HD brains (Berg et al., 2024).
evidence: This is based on western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and comparison to human HD brain (Berg et al., 2024).

claim: In general, autophagy alterations at the protein level, as can be detected by immunoblotting, are mild in TRGL/Q175 even at 17-mo-old.
source: Together, our data suggest that, in general, autophagy alterations at the protein level, as can be detected by immunoblotting, are mild in TRGL/Q175 even at 17-mo-old (See Discussion).
evidence: This is a summary of the western blotting findings.

claim: NIIs were not observed in WT neurons but were detected in ~10% striatal neurons of Q175 mice at 17-mo of age.
source: To assess possible ultrastructural pathologies, we conducted an EM study for Q175 vs WT at 17-mo of age. As predicted, NIIs were not observed in WT neurons (Figure 3B, left panel) but were detected (Figure 3B, right panel, red circle) in ~10% striatal neurons of Q175 mice.
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Gross accumulation of AVs was not observed in Q175 at 17-mo of age, except that larger sized (>1 µm) lipofuscin granules modestly increased in number in Q175 compared to WT.
source: Different from the substantial accumulation of AVs including lipofuscin granules in late stage human HD brain (e.g., HD4) (Berg et al., 2024), we did not observe gross accumulation of AVs in Q175 at this old age, except that quantitative analysis of EM images revealed that larger sized (>1 µm) lipofuscin granules (Figure 3B, right panel, arrow) modestly increased in number in Q175 compared to WT [WT: 113 lipofuscin/420 neurons (n=6 mice), i.e., 27 lipofuscin/100 neurons; Q175: 228 lipofuscin/586 neurons (n=9 mice), i.e., 39 lipofuscin/100 neurons; Unpaired t-test, Two-tailed p-value <0.01; Bar graph not shown].
evidence: This is supported by quantitative EM data.

claim: These EM findings suggest that ultrastructural autophagy alterations in the ALP were mild in Q175 even at an older age.
source: Thus, these EM findings suggest that ultrastructural autophagy alterations in the ALP were mild in Q175 even at an older age.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EM findings.

claim: The intensity of DARPP-32-IR significantly diminished in TRGL/Q175 compared to TRGL at 17-mo of age.
source: To investigate potential neurodegeneration in our model, brain sections from 17-mo-old mice were double-labeled with the medium spiny neuron marker DARPP-32 (dopamine- and cAMP-regulated phosphoprotein, 32 kDa)(Ouimet et al., 1998) and a general neuronal marker NeuN. We found that the intensity of DARPP-32-IR significantly diminished in TRGL/Q175 compared to TRGL (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: There were no alterations in NeuN-IR, including Area Covered and the Number of NeuN-positive neurons, in TRGL/Q175 compared to TRGL at 17-mo of age.
source: However, there were no alterations in NeuN-IR, including Area Covered and the Number of NeuN-positive neurons (Figure 4A and B), and there were clear examples of neurons showing strong NeuN signal but faint or no DARPP-32 signal (Figure 4A, arrows).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: There were clear examples of neurons showing strong NeuN signal but faint or no DARPP-32 signal in TRGL/Q175 at 17-mo of age.
source: However, there were no alterations in NeuN-IR, including Area Covered and the Number of NeuN-positive neurons (Figure 4A and B), and there were clear examples of neurons showing strong NeuN signal but faint or no DARPP-32 signal (Figure 4A, arrows).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The finding is consistent with other studies in Q175 and Q140 mice where neuronal loss was not found even though a reduction in DARPP-32 was seen in the same study, and that neuronal loss only occurred quite late, e.g., around 2 y of age.
source: Such a finding is consistent with other studies in Q175 and Q140 mice where neuronal loss was not found even though a reduction in DARPP-32 was seen in the same study, and that neuronal loss only occurred quite late, e.g., around 2 y of age (Deng et al., 2021; Hickey et al., 2008; Peng et al., 2016; Rothe et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior studies (Deng et al., 2021; Hickey et al., 2008; Peng et al., 2016; Rothe et al., 2015).

claim: The data support the notion that changes in DARPP-32 may indicate alterations in its protein level and a loss of phenotype pattern, which is a potentially common prelude to neuronal loss in other neuronal cell types.
source: Thus, our data support the notion that changes in DARPP-32 may indicate alterations in its protein level and a loss of phenotype pattern, which is a potentially common prelude to neuronal loss in other neuronal cell types, e.g., basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (Jiang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, supported by a citation (Jiang et al., 2022).

claim: All doses of INK tested, from 2.5 mg/kg (mpk) to 10-mpk, exhibited target engagement as revealed by the reductions in the protein levels of mTOR targets in WT mice.
source: As a prelude to investigate effects of pharmacological autophagy stimulation with a mTORi, INK, on TRGL/Q175 mice, we first performed a safety, pharmacokinetic, and pharmacodynamic evaluation of INK in 6-mo-old WT mice, administered via oral gavage. The WB results (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) indicated that all doses tested, from 2.5 mg/kg (mpk) to 10-mpk, exhibited target engagement as revealed by the reductions in the protein levels of mTOR targets, i.e., p-ULK1 (S757, phosphorylated by mTOR), p-p70S6K (not shown), or phosphorylated S6 ribosomal protein (p-S6, at S240/244), implying high BBB permeability of this compound and target engagement.
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The results imply high BBB permeability of INK and target engagement.
source: The WB results (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) indicated that all doses tested, from 2.5 mg/kg (mpk) to 10-mpk, exhibited target engagement as revealed by the reductions in the protein levels of mTOR targets, i.e., p-ULK1 (S757, phosphorylated by mTOR), p-p70S6K (not shown), or phosphorylated S6 ribosomal protein (p-S6, at S240/244), implying high BBB permeability of this compound and target engagement.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the western blotting findings.

claim: Measurements for the levels of INK in cerebellar homogenates of WT mice treated with 1, 3, and 10-mpk INK revealed dose-dependent brain levels of INK.
source: Consistently, measurements for the levels of INK in cerebellar homogenates of WT mice treated with 1, 3, and 10-mpk INK revealed dose-dependent brain levels of INK (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacokinetic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Target engagement of INK in TRGL/Q175 was verified by decreased levels of p-mTOR (S2481), p-ULK1 (S757) and p-S6 (S240) in brain homogenates from INK-treated TRGL/Q175 compared to Veh-treated TRGL/Q175.
source: We then decided on an oral gavage treatment regimen for INK as 4-mpk, daily, for 3 wk, to be administered in 6-mo-old TRGL/Q175. The brains from the mice (7-mo of age after the 3 wk treatment duration) were then analyzed by multiple experimental approaches. By immunoblotting, target engagement was verified, as indicated by decreased levels of p-mTOR (S2481, autophosphorylation site), p-ULK1 (S757) and p-S6 (S240) in brain homogenates from INK-treated TRGL/Q175 compared to Veh-treated TRGL/Q175 (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: There were INK-induced changes in marker proteins located downstream of autophagy induction, including increased levels of p-ATG14 in INK-treated samples.
source: Additionally, there were also INK-induced changes in marker proteins located downstream of autophagy induction, including, for example, increased levels of p-ATG14 in INK-treated samples (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Although INK did not induce any alterations in the transgene product tfLC3-I or -II, there was a trend of decreased endogenous LC3-I, leading to a statistically significant increase in the ratio of LC3-II/I.
source: It is interesting that although INK did not induce any alterations in the transgene product tfLC3-I or -II, there was a trend of decreased endogenous LC3-I, leading to a statistically significant increase in the ratio of LC3-II/I, and such a result in LC3-I reduction was reproduced in a repeated experiment (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The pilot study in WT mice and the actual study in TRGL/Q175 mice together established mTORi INK's BBB permeability, target engagement, and ability to modify molecular events in the ALP.
source: Thus, the pilot study in WT mice and the actual study in TRGL/Q175 mice together established mTORi INK's BBB permeability, target engagement, and ability to modify molecular events in the ALP.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the INK dosing studies.

claim: The analysis in striatal neurons revealed reversal of the two main ALP alterations by INK treatment: the pre-existing abnormally lowered LY number in TRGL/Q175-Veh was reversed by INK treatment.
source: We took advantage of the tfLC3 construct reporting in vivo autophagy flux (Lee et al., 2019) to assess INK effects on AV/LY subtypes in TRGL/Q175. Confocal images from INK- or Veh-treated TRGL/Q175 and Veh-treated TRGL brain sections of 7-mo-old mice, immuno-stained with anti-CTSD antibody and detected with a third fluorophore, were collected (Figure 6A) and processed for hue-angle based quantitative analysis using the protocol described previously (Lee et al., 2019). The analysis in striatal neurons (Figure 6B) revealed reversal of the two main ALP alterations. First, the pre-existing abnormally lowered LY number in TRGL/Q175-Veh (Figure 6B, LY group, red vs green), was reversed by INK treatment (Figure 6B, LY group, red vs blue).
evidence: This is supported by hue angle-based analysis data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: INK reduced the number of AL in TRGL/Q175-Veh compared to TRGL-Veh, implying improved AL clearance and likely providing the basis for restoration of normal LY number.
source: Second, INK reduced the number of AL in TRGL/Q175-Veh compared to TRGL-Veh (Figure 6B, AL group, red vs blue), implying improved AL clearance and likely providing the basis for restoration of normal LY number.
evidence: This is supported by hue angle-based analysis data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The data suggest that autophagy phenotype in 7-mo Q175 is measurable but milder than that in the 17-mo-old mice and that INK has the potential to modulate the autophagy pathway and restore normal function at this mild disease stage.
source: Together, the data suggest that autophagy phenotype in 7-mo Q175 is measurable but milder than that in the 17-mo-old mice shown in Figure 3A and that INK has the potential to modulate the autophagy pathway and restore normal function at this mild disease stage.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hue angle-based analysis findings.

claim: HD-like pathology such as mHTT IBs and associated protein aggregation of adaptor proteins, p62, and Ub, was ameliorated by INK treatment.
source: Importantly, we found that HD-like pathology such as mHTT IBs and associated protein aggregation of adaptor proteins, p62, and Ub, was ameliorated by INK treatment.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings shown in Figure 7.

claim: Confocal images demonstrated that mHTT positive particles/inclusions were substantially reduced in INK-treated 7-mo-old TRGL/Q175, compared to Veh-treated TRGL/Q175 mice.
source: Confocal images demonstrated that mHTT positive particles/inclusions were substantially reduced in INK-treated 7-mo-old TRGL/Q175, compared to Veh-treated TRGL/Q175 mice (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: p62-IR and Ub-IR also changed in a similar trend to mHTT-IR after INK treatment, consistent with the high degree of colocalization of mHTT/p62/Ub signals.
source: Moreover, p62-IR or Ub-IR also changed in a similar trend (Figure 7A), consistent with the high degree of colocalization of mHTT/p62/Ub signals shown in Figure 2A.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Quantitative analysis confirmed statistically significant decreases in the Total Area Covered by mHTT- and p62-signals after INK treatment.
source: The corresponding quantitative analysis, shown as Area Covered by either mHTT-, p62-, or Ub-IR on a per cell basis, confirmed statistically significant decreases in the Total Area Covered by mHTT- and p62-signals (Figure 7B1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B1.

claim: The results collectively suggest decreased mHTT-, p62-, or Ub-IR in treated compared to untreated TRGL/Q175, implying that INK treatment was able to promote the clearance of mHTT and related receptor proteins p62 and/or Ub.
source: With the assistance of the endogenous tfLC3 signal (particularly the mRFP signal) in the TRGL to identify the association status of the mHTT-, p62-, or Ub-IR with AVs, the images were additionally quantified to generate the separated 'Area Covered by the AV-associated Form' (Figure 7B2) and 'Area Covered by the AV-unassociated Form' (Figure 7B3) of mHTT-, p62-, or Ub- signals. The results collectively suggest decreased mHTT-, p62-, or Ub-IR in treated compared to untreated TRGL/Q175, implying that INK treatment was able to promote the clearance of mHTT and related receptor proteins p62 and/or Ub.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B1-B3.

claim: The group of TRGL/Q175-Veh, even at 7-mo of age, already exhibited a diminished DARPP-32-IR signal compared to that in TRGL-Veh.
source: Finally, we evaluated neurodegenerative changes by employing DARPP-32 IHC on brain sections of Veh-treated or INK-treated TRGL/Q175. Similar to what was found in 17-mo-old mice (Figure 4), the group of TRGL/Q175-Veh, even at this young age (7-mo), already exhibited a diminished DARPP-32-IR signal compared to that in TRGL-Veh (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: No differences between the untreated and INK-treated TRGL/Q175 groups were established by quantitative analysis of DARPP-32-IR.
source: However, no differences between the untreated and INK-treated TRGL/Q175 groups were established by quantitative analysis (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: The result suggests a lack of effectiveness of INK in reversing the pre-existing DARPP-32 phenotype, implying that earlier intervention may be necessary.
source: Thus, the result suggests a lack of effectiveness of INK in reversing this pre-existing phenotype, implying that earlier intervention may be necessary (Marchionini et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DARPP-32 findings, supported by a citation (Marchionini et al., 2022).

claim: WT HTT participates in normal autophagy by releasing ULK1 via mTOR inhibition and serving as a scaffold to facilitate cargo sequestration by enhancing p62 interaction with LC3 and ubiquitinated cargos.
source: Previous studies in cell and animal models have documented roles of HTT and mHTT in autophagy in relation to HD [for reviews, see Croce and Yamamoto, 2019; Klionsky et al., 2021; Martin et al., 2015]. WT HTT participates in normal autophagy by releasing ULK1 via mTOR inhibition and serving as a scaffold to facilitate cargo sequestration by enhancing p62 interaction with LC3 and ubiquitinated cargos (Ochaba et al., 2014; Rui et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Ochaba et al., 2014; Rui et al., 2015).

claim: mHTT in HD may activate autophagy by sequestering and thus inhibiting mTOR.
source: mHTT in HD may activate autophagy by sequestering and thus inhibiting mTOR (Ravikumar et al., 2004).
